This is a singularly important contribution. Rarely are we handed a new way of listening to our patients that expands and transforms how we understand our work in the manner that Dr. Maurice Apprey achieves in this edited collection of his work, Transgenerational Haunting in Psychoanalysis: Toxic Errands. Apprey invites us to consider what happens if self-states designated as Not-Me widen to include those inherited familial/cultural traumas that a particular self was not alive for, yet nonetheless were imprinted on them psychically. He aptly renames the legacy of unresolved past wounds “toxic errands” and “haunts,” and he utilizes his psychoanalytic praxis to move these ghostly inheritances into less obstructive injuries for his patients, applying the same model to address inter-ethnic conflict between groups more generally. Morris Eagle’s Toward a Unified Psychoanalytic Theory: Foundation in a Revised and Expanded Ego Psychology mounts a far-reaching and deeply researched argument that many readers will find heartening and some might find galling. To the author’s great credit, this book is written with all of us in mind. According to Eagle, the proliferation of analytic schools has created a crisis of coherence for our field, and our strongest solution is a mass return to and revision of ego psychology, the one psychoanalytic school that he feels offers an adequate and unifying theory of mind.

When I first encountered this book, I bristled at the premise—that the cure for our splintered field was to lay down our petty allegiances and gather in the ostensibly neutral territory that happened to be Eagle’s own turf. As I followed his argument, however, I was struck by his earnest, rigorous attempts to incorporate, rather than dismiss, the essential contributions of object relations, self-psychology, and interpersonal and relational analysis. Eagle works here like a patriarchal homebuilder, adding new wings to an original structure in the hopes that all analysts might find comfortable rooms of their own to come home to more often. Whether these rooms are adequate for permanent residence, as opposed to occasional reunions, may be another matter.

An important aspect of Clara Thompson’s pioneering work in psychoanalysis stems from her personal analysis with Sandor Ferenczi. Her contributions, deeply rooted in her own experiences of emotional trauma and psychic pain, led to an innovative clinical perspective that emphasized empathy and mutuality. This approach challenged traditional Freudian methods and laid the groundwork for the interpersonal/relational turn in psychoanalytic practice. Thompson’s legacy continues to shape contemporary psychoanalytic thought, underscoring the significance of empathic connections and the influence of the analyst’s personality in therapy.

Psychotherapy with the elderly, trauma, Holocaust, body-mind, dance/movement psychotherapy

Individuals who survived the Holocaust as infants are now in their senior years. Having carried lifelong wounds—stemming both from exposure to horrors and from the absence of caregivers to meet basic developmental needs—many of these survivors hold early experiences that remain wordless, stored internally without expression or meaning. Dance/movement psychotherapy encourages patients to engage with embodied knowledge through movement, in parallel with verbal processing of experiences in motion. This integration bridges implicit and explicit realms, supporting the development of a more cohesive sense of self and enabling the processing of early traumatic experiences. Through a case study, we will illustrate interventions that combine bodily focus with verbal symbolism as pathways to growth and tranquility in later life.

This article depicts the case of a young woman whose presentation, exhibitionistic and featuring her physicality, initially drew attention away from the vulnerabilities most in need of clinical attention. I find Fairbairn’s theory brimming with treasures of great value in the therapeutic setting. Whereas pregnancy in the analytic treatment space has been a topic of discussion in several articles in the psychoanalytic literature, it is most often from the perspective of the patient or the pregnant analyst. This article discusses the experience of the non-carrying therapist whose partner is pregnant. A case discussion, highlighting the period of the work with a patient prior to the disclosure of the pregnancy, is presented. This article reviews prior analytic literature on pregnancy, and describes pregnancy as a transformative process that typically involves regression and a re-experiencing of events from early in one’s history. The result for this case is that when the patient and non-carrying analyst regress together, they co-create a more secure analytic attachment, deepening their work. Theoretical ideas concerning unconscious communication, telepathic dreams, and gestation are presented to help the analyst and reader understand the unique experience of working as an expectant non-carrying analyst.

With The Authority of Tenderness, Paul Williams (2022, 2010, 2013) provides the third volume of his trilogy that began with The Fifth Principle and was followed by Scum, and it is an emotionally powerful addition to the trilogy. All three books contain, in part, a description of the traumatic experience of a child and adolescent who suffered extensive emotional deprivation and abuse by his parents. All these works combine both fiction and autobiography, which are most of the time challenging to distinguish. In this series, Williams offers an in-depth understanding of the potentially devastating impact of early childhood trauma. Leaning heavily on Winnicottian ideas of holding and surviving the destruction of objects, Williams writes eloquently about clinical sequelae and reveals an analytic stance that he suggests is essential for the treatment of childhood traumatogenic disturbances of the self.

As was the case in the two previous volumes, The Authority of Tenderness is narrated by a psychoanalyst. Jung was fascinated by many aspects of the uncanny and described them from the psychological perspective that he developed. For example, he saw the uncanny in elements of the occult, in the occurrence of synchronicity, and in the way that everyday complexes of the psyche go bump in the night. Common to all of these is that the unconscious itself has a prospective and intelligent aspect, and when this cannot be attributed to the ego, that is just what we mean by the uncanny. That is, something happens mysteriously without our intention, but with purpose and apparent action at a distance.

Uncanny, telepathy, truth, mystery, contemporary physics, thought-transference

Emily Dickinson’s poetic injunction to “tell all the truth but tell it slant” offers an orientation toward a topic that has long been highly controversial within psychoanalytic theory and practice: the exploration of uncanny clinical moments and their implications. Although Freud was fascinated with this topic, his fear of its potential to unravel both individual and collective certainty drove his interest and that of psychoanalysts after him underground. Using clinical and theoretical material as well as models within contemporary physics, this paper suggests that uncanny moments invite us to glimpse a profound underlying interconnectedness which asks us to bear both fear and awe.

Telepathy, intuition, uncanny, countertransference, mutual, boundarylessness

This article compares two clinical cases depicting varying types of telepathic transmission. De Peyer illustrates differing reactions that can be triggered in the same analyst, depending on the nature and circumstance of the anomalous communication. The first case illustrates a series of uncanny transmissions culminating in a telepathic dream of the patient’s, which depicts, in detail, a medical emergency that transpired in the analyst’s home. De Peyer describes the sense of boundarylessness that this dream produced, as if the patient were “trespassing in her mind.” This is contrasted with a second case in which when asked by the patient to come up with a name to call her lover, de Peyer spontaneously chooses a name that has tremendous symbolic meaning to the patient, unlocking otherwise inaccessible developmental material. De Peyer illustrates ways that anomalous transmissions generate varied reactions in the analyst, yet can often serve as “portals” leading to positive clinical transformation.

In this paper, we outline a processual notion of meaning and sensemaking and use this to frame a semiotic reading of some core concepts in psychoanalytic theory and practice. We review the implications of the processual notion of meaning for psychoanalytic theory.

He is president of the Stephen Mitchell Relational Study Center and is editor emeritus of Psychoanalytic Dialogues.
Uncanny, dialogue of unconsciouses, thought transference, anomalous experience, imagination, dreaming

This paper considers the idea of the “uncanny,” in psychoanalysis from two different vantage points. First, I consider Freud’s monograph on the “uncanny,” in which he explored the experience of the uncanny as representing an intrapsychic, one-person phenomenon, linking a familiar feeling to the presence or resonance of the unconscious as it is becoming manifest in an individual. Then I consider forms of “uncanniness” that constitute two unconsciouses at play in an interpersonal or intersubjective, two person field, reflecting the special evocative power manifest in and generated by unconscious to unconscious communication, representing forms of what Ferenczi considered to be a dialogue of unconsciouses. Examples of both kinds of “uncanniness” are considered, in and outside of the therapy experience.

Uncanny, unconscious, Jung, interpersonal psychoanalysis, intersubjectivity, synchronicity

Freud dismissed Jung, who had been his heir-apparent, from his inner circle because of their differing ideas about the uncanny and Jung’s interest in the occult. Due to this rupture, many of Jung’s seminal ideas were lost to psychoanalysis. However, recent theoretical concepts in our field, including intersubjectivity and the intergenerational transmission of trauma, have led some psychoanalysts to reconsider the uncanny in their clinical work. Uncanny experiences are understood by Jungians as the central conduit to the unconscious. This paper will compare how the unconscious is conceptualized by Jungians and by Interpersonal and Relational psychoanalysts. Differing ideas about the unconscious are foundational to how the uncanny is now being understood in contemporary psychoanalysis generally and in Interpersonal and Relational Psychoanalysis in particular.

This essay endeavors to situate notions of transcendence historically, philosophically, religiously, and experientially. Thereby arises a case that is fundamental to the clinical process of psychoanalysis is a transcendent effort to alter lived reality, the very scope of being. More than for symptom reduction, improved adaptation, or cure, psychoanalysis works to loosen those transferential habits of egotistical mind that defensively constrict one’s ways of being in the world. Elements of uncanny or mystical experience and of psychedelic therapeusis are pertinent to this transcendent viewpoint, this “overmind.” Transcendence of egotistic self becomes an escape from dualistic self-versus-other, an escape toward freedom, humanely being with, for, and fundamentally of one another.

Buddhism, compassion, empathy, intersubjectivity, nonduality, uncanny

Accessing empathy and compassion in the therapeutic encounter helps us attune to that which is spoken—and as such transpiring in the dual plane—and to that which is unspoken and transferred between therapist and patient in a nondual state of oneness. Specifically, empathy operates on the dual plane where self and other can be discerned and compassion operates on the nondual plane where the distinctions of self and other soften into a state of inter-being. Listening for this realm in which we “inter-are” (Nhat Hanh, 1988) enables us to notice and to make use of the unspoken and unthought. With this understanding, the meaning of the uncanny shifts from being an unusual and eerie experience to being an ever-present intersubjective experience that transpires at the interpenetration of dual and nondual modes of being.

Sue Grand PHD

Fascism, authoritarianism, dictatorship, masculine narcissism, gender fluidity, women

Fascism is resurgent around the globe; its atrocities seem to be erased from historic memory. In this article, the author probes the eroticized field that exists between fascism’s leaders and its followers. The article proposes that a subliminal erotic seduction is foundational to fascist structures. This phenomena is characterized by a veneer of purity and moralism, which ignites, and conceals a gendered web of perversion. The author argues that fascism writes erotic law and ignites transgressions of its own law. All of this sustains phallic mythologies of hyper-hetero-masculine supremacy and prowess. To maintain this fragile, collective masculine narcissism, fascism relies on a split off, externalized category of ‘deviance,’ which is persecuted. In exploring these arrangements, the article emphasizes the dread of, hatred for, and control of women. Finally, the author questions fascism’s construction of the gender fluid fascist woman whose support is vital to these movements.

Jill Salberg PHD

Jill Salberg

She is on the Editorial Board of Psychoanalytic Quarterly, Associate Editor of Psychoanalytic Dialogues and a Reviewer for The International Journal of Psychoanalysis. Her books are: Editor of and contributor to two books: Good Enough Endings: Breaks, Interruptions and Terminations from Contemporary Relational Perspectives (2010), and Psychoanalytic Credos: Personal and Professional Journeys of Psychoanalysts (2022). amnesia, mourning, trauma, witnessing, fascism

This article suggests that “fascism amnesia” has occurred when the world no longer remembers enough about the antecedents and repercussions of its history. This nonmemory can fail to prevent its recurrence. Reviewing what is happening in the United States and in the world, the author argues that these are all examples of reemerging deeply oppressive fascistic forces and the ways that regimes of power exert control over minorities, their most vulnerable citizens. The author further believes that the forgetting of history can be understood as part of the phenomenon of transgenerational transmission of trauma, where the unfinished work or wounds of one generation get passed down to the next. Further, it will be argued that to break or interrupt this transmission, a bearing witness needs to happen. An example is offered of the Abuelas of Plaza de Mayo in Argentina, whose ongoing mourning and the persistence of memory offers successive generations an entry into the process of “continuing mentalizing.” Such witnessing needs to be in the service of defying and refusing fascistic amnesia.
